title: Texas HB 149: Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA)

covered_actors: Any person who promotes, advertises, or conducts business in Texas, produces a product or service used by Texas residents, or develops or deploys an artificial intelligence system in Texas (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 551.002)

Private-sector AI developers and deployers, personal-data processors handling data collected, stored, or processed by AI systems (§ 541.104(a)), and entities capturing or storing biometric identifiers for commercial or AI-training purposes (§ 503.001)

Texas governmental entities and state agencies (departments, commissions, boards, offices, authorities, and political subdivisions, excluding hospital districts and public institutions of higher education under § 552.001(3))
Licensed health care service and treatment providers deploying AI in patient care (§ 552.051(f))
AI regulatory sandbox program participants approved by the Texas Department of Information Resources (DIR) and applicable state licensing agencies (Chapter 553)
prohibited_practices: Developing or deploying an AI system that intentionally aims to incite or encourage a person to commit physical self-harm (including suicide), harm another person, or engage in criminal activity (§ 552.052)

Governmental entities using or deploying an AI system to evaluate or classify persons based on social behavior or personal characteristics to assign a social score resulting in unrelated or disproportionate detrimental treatment or constitutional/statutory rights infringement (§ 552.053)

Governmental entities developing or deploying an AI system to uniquely identify a specific individual via biometric data or targeted/untargeted scraping of internet or public media without consent where it infringes constitutional or statutory rights, and commercial capture/storage of biometric identifiers from scraped public media not posted by the individual (§ 552.054, § 503.001(b-1))
Developing or deploying an AI system with the sole intent to infringe, restrict, or otherwise impair individual rights guaranteed under the U.S. Constitution (§ 552.055)

Developing or deploying an AI system with the intent to unlawfully discriminate against a protected class (race, color, national origin, sex, age, religion, or disability) in violation of state or federal law, noting disparate impact alone does not prove discriminatory intent (§ 552.056)

Developing or distributing an AI system with the sole intent of producing or distributing child sexual abuse material (Penal Code § 43.26) or unlawful sexually explicit deepfakes (Penal Code § 21.165), or intentionally developing/distributing an AI system engaging in text-based sexually explicit conversations while impersonating or imitating a child under age 18 (§ 552.057)
Political subdivisions adopting local ordinances, resolutions, rules, or regulations governing the use of AI systems (statewide local preemption, § 552.003)

enforcement_authorities: Texas Attorney General (exclusive enforcement authority for Chapter 552, online consumer complaint portal, Civil Investigative Demands, 60-day notice-and-cure, civil penalties, and injunctive relief)

Applicable Texas state licensing/regulatory agencies (license suspension, probation, revocation, and up to $100,000 penalty upon AG finding and recommendation under § 552.106; co-oversight of regulatory sandbox participants)

Texas Department of Information Resources (DIR) (administration and oversight of the 36-month AI regulatory sandbox program under Chapter 553, administrative support for the Texas AI Council, and state agency AI inventories under Gov. Code §§ 2054.068, 2054.0965)
Texas Department of Insurance (exclusive oversight of the business of insurance under § 552.002(2))
Texas Artificial Intelligence Council (advisory and non-binding oversight/reporting body under Chapter 554) and Texas Sunset Advisory Commission (state agency AI review under Gov. Code § 325.011(15))
compliance_deadlines: 2026-01-01: General effective date of Texas HB 149 (TRAIGA) (Section 10)
2026-09-01 (not later than September 1, 2026): Texas Attorney General must publish online consumer complaint mechanism and information required under § 552.102 (Section 8)

60-day statutory cure period: Violators receive 60 days after written AG notice of violation to cure, submit written certification with supporting documentation, and update internal policies before AG suit (§ 552.104(b))

Up to 36 months (extendable for good cause): Maximum regulatory sandbox testing/deployment period with mandatory quarterly participant reports to DIR and annual DIR reports to the legislature (§§ 553.053, 553.102, 553.103)
Healthcare AI disclosure: Must be provided not later than the date service or treatment is first provided (or as soon as reasonably possible in emergencies) (§ 552.051(f))
policy_extraction.penalties_summary: Uncured violations of Chapter 552 carry state civil penalties enforceable exclusively by the Texas Attorney General (no private right of action): $10,000–$12,000 per curable violation (or breach of a cure statement), $80,000–$200,000 per uncurable violation, and $2,000–$40,000 per day for continuing violations, plus injunctive relief, attorney's fees, and investigative costs (§ 552.105). Following an AG violation finding and recommendation, state licensing agencies may suspend, place on probation, or revoke licenses/authorizations and impose additional monetary penalties up to $100,000 (§ 552.106). Commercial misuse of biometric identifiers captured for AI training triggers existing § 503.001 biometric statutory penalties. Rebuttable presumption of reasonable care, no penalties for undeployed systems, and liability safe harbors apply for third-party misuse, red-team/adversarial testing discovery, and substantial compliance with the NIST Generative AI Profile.
policy_extraction.implementation_notes: Enacted in the 89th Texas Legislature (signed June 22, 2025; effective January 1, 2026), TRAIGA adds Subtitle D (Chapters 551–554) to Title 11 of the Texas Business & Commerce Code while amending Texas biometric (§ 503.001), data privacy (§ 541.104), and state-agency IT/Sunset statutes. Rather than imposing European-style risk-tier compliance mandates on private developers, Texas pairs narrow intent-based red-line prohibitions (self-harm/violence/crime incitement, governmental social scoring, rights-infringing governmental biometric scraping, sole-intent constitutional infringement, intentional protected-class discrimination, CSAM/deepfake/child-impersonating sexual chatbots) with statewide local preemption, a 36-month deregulatory AI sandbox administered by DIR, safe harbors for red-teaming and NIST AI RMF compliance, and a seven-member advisory Texas AI Council barred from issuing binding rules. Section 9 conditions mandatory state-agency implementation duties on specific legislative appropriations.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: Texas HB 149 (TRAIGA) is led by an innovation enablement rationale, opening Subtitle D with the purpose to facilitate and advance responsible AI development and use, establishing a 36-month regulatory sandbox waiving state licensing requirements to encourage safe testing across healthcare, finance, education, and public services, preempting local AI regulations, carving out AI training from biometric consent rules, creating NIST framework and red-teaming safe harbors, and directing the Texas AI Council to identify laws impeding innovation and guard against regulatory capture. Fundamental rights is a strong secondary rationale reflected in explicit prohibitions against infringing U.S. Constitutional rights, free-speech protection, bans on governmental social scoring and rights-infringing biometric scraping, and bans on intentional protected-class discrimination. Consumer and public safety forms a co-present secondary pillar aimed at protecting individuals from known and foreseeable AI risks, prohibiting AI systems intended to incite self-harm, violence, crime, or child sexual exploitation, requiring transparent consumer and patient AI disclosures, and authorizing sandbox removal when systems pose undue risk to public safety or welfare.

This subtitle shall be broadly construed and applied to promote its
underlying purposes, which are to:
(1)
facilitate and advance the responsible
development and use of artificial intelligence systems;

(3)
identify existing laws and regulations that impede
innovation in the development of artificial intelligence systems
and recommend appropriate reforms;

A person may
not develop or deploy an artificial intelligence system with the
sole intent for the artificial intelligence system to infringe,
restrict, or otherwise impair an individual's rights guaranteed
under the United States Constitution.

A person may not develop or deploy an artificial
intelligence system with the intent to unlawfully discriminate
against a protected class in violation of state or federal law.

(2)
protect individuals and groups of individuals from
known and reasonably foreseeable risks associated with artificial
intelligence systems;

(2)
encourage responsible deployment of artificial
intelligence systems while balancing the need for consumer
protection, privacy, and public safety;
